blocks.content: German nouns change form depending on their role in the sentence. At A1 level we focus on nominative (subject) and accusative (direct object).
Nominative — the subject
The subject performs the action. Ask: "Who or what is doing the verb?" Nouns after sein (to be) are also nominative.
Accusative — the direct object
The direct object receives the action. Ask: "Who or what is being verbed?" Only masculine articles change: der → den, ein → einen.

blocks.note: Er = subject · ein Buch = object (neuter, no change)

blocks.content:
Nominative: subjects; after sein
Accusative: direct objects; after accusative prepositions (durch, für, ohne…)
Personal pronouns also change in the accusative case. Only ich → mich and du → dich change among the singular pronouns you use most at A1.
These prepositions always take the accusative case. The noun that follows must be in accusative form.

durch (through)
für (for)
gegen (against)
ohne (without)
um (around, at [time])
entlang (along — follows the noun)

blocks.de: Das Geschenk ist für den Mann.

blocks.content: Sein (to be) and heißen (to be called) are irregular but essential from day one.

blocks.de: Ich bin Student. Ich heiße Anna.
blocks.note: Use sein for identity/ origin; heißen for your name

blocks.content: Modal verbs express ability, permission, obligation, or desire. The main verb goes to the end in infinitive form.

können (can)
müssen (must)
wollen (want to)
dürfen (may)
sollen (should)
Some verbs change their stem vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms (and du-form only for some). The pattern is fixed per verb — learn them with the infinitive.

e → i: geben → du gibst
e → ie: sehen → du siehst
a → ä: fahren → du fährst
Negate verbs with nicht (not the verb itself). Negate nouns with kein (not a/ no + noun) — kein declines like ein.

blocks.de: Ich trinke nicht Kaffee. / Ich trinke keinen Kaffee.
blocks.note: nicht = general negation · kein = "no/not a" + noun

blocks.content: Basic phrases for meeting people. Formal situations use Sie; friends and peers use du.

Guten Tag! — Good day
Wie heißen Sie? / Wie heißt du? — What's your name?
Ich heiße … — My name is …
Woher kommen Sie? — Where are you from?
Freut mich. — Nice to meet you.

blocks.de: Guten Tag! Ich heiße Maria. Woher kommen Sie?

blocks.content: Question words (W-words) come first, then the verb (V2 rule). Yes/no questions start with the verb.

wer — who
was — what
wo — where
wann — when
warum — why
wie — how
woher — from where
wohin — to where
The imperative gives commands. Du-form often drops the -st ending; Sie-form uses the infinitive + Sie.

Komm! / Kommen Sie! — Come!
Lies! / Lesen Sie! — Read!
Seid leise! — Be quiet! (ihr-form)
The dative case marks the indirect object — the recipient or beneficiary. Ask: "To/for whom?" Masculine and neuter articles become dem; feminine die → der; plural die → den (+ n on noun sometimes).

blocks.de: Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch.

blocks.content: Certain verbs always take a dative object (no accusative). Learn them as chunks.

helfen (+ dat.) — to help
gehören (+ dat.) — to belong to
danken (+ dat.) — to thank
gefallen (+ dat.) — to please
antworten (+ dat.) — to answer
Quick reference for the three cases at A2 level.

rows: Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch.

blocks.de: Die Frau gibt dem Kind einen Apfel.
blocks.note: Die Frau (nom.) · dem Kind (dat.) · einen Apfel (acc.)

blocks.content: Der-words (dieser, jeder, welcher, mancher…) and ein-words (mein, dein, kein…) decline like articles in each case.

blocks.de: Ich kaufe meinem Bruder ein Geschenk.

blocks.content: Wechselpräpositionen (two-way prepositions) take accusative for movement (wohin?) or dative for location (wo?).
an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen
More practice with the wohin/wo distinction. Movement = accusative; static position = dative.

blocks.de: Sie stellt die Vase auf den Tisch.
Die Vase steht auf dem Tisch.

blocks.content: Combined contexts: describe where something is and where it is going using the same preposition with different cases.

blocks.de: Das Bild hängt an der Wand. / Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand.
blocks.note: an der Wand (dat.) · an die Wand (acc.)

blocks.content: Time-Manner-Place (Te-Ka-Mo): temporal, then manner, then place. In main clauses the conjugated verb stays in position 2.

blocks.de: Ich fahre heute mit dem Bus nach Berlin.
blocks.note: heute (time) · mit dem Bus (manner) · nach Berlin (place)

blocks.content: The Perfekt (spoken past) = haben or sein + past participle (Partizip II). Most verbs use haben; movement/change-of-state verbs use sein.

Regular: ge- + stem + -t (gemacht, gespielt)
Irregular: ge- + changed stem + -en (gesehen, gegangen)
Separable: prefix stays before ge- (eingekauft)
Common sein-verbs in Perfekt: gehen, kommen, fahren, fliegen, bleiben, werden. The participle agrees in number with the subject when using sein.
Präteritum is the written/narrative past. At A2, focus on sein, haben, and modal verbs — they are used more in Präteritum than in speech.

blocks.de: Es war kalt und ich hatte keine Zeit.

blocks.content: Weak (regular) verbs add -te endings: machen → machte. Strong verbs change the stem: gehen → ging, sehen → sah.

blocks.de: Er ging ins Kino und kaufte Popcorn.

blocks.content: Reflexive verbs use a reflexive pronoun (mich, dich, sich…) that refers back to the subject. Many daily-routine verbs are reflexive.

sich waschen — to wash (oneself)
sich anziehen — to get dressed
sich freuen — to be glad
sich interessieren — to be interested

blocks.de: Ich wasche mich. / Du wäschst dich.

blocks.content: Some reflexive verbs take an optional dative object. Accusative reflexive is most common at A2.

blocks.de: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.

blocks.content: Separable prefixes (an-, auf-, ein-, mit-, vor-…) detach and move to the end in main clauses.

blocks.de: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.

blocks.content: Werden means "to become" and is also used as a helper for Futur I and passive (later levels).
Coordinating conjunctions (und, aber, oder, denn, sondern) do not change word order. Subordinating conjunctions (weil, dass, wenn, ob…) send the conjugated verb to the end.

blocks.de: Ich lerne, weil ich die Prüfung bestehen will.

blocks.content: Common subordinating conjunctions: weil (because), dass (that), wenn (if/when), ob (whether), als (when in past).

blocks.de: Er sagt, dass er müde ist.

blocks.content: Time expressions often come early in the sentence (after the verb or in position 1). Use accusative for definite time spans, dative for dates and seasons in some contexts.

blocks.de: Am Montag gehe ich ins Kino.

blocks.content: Possessive articles (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer) decline like ein in all cases.

blocks.de: Das ist mein Bruder. / Ich sehe meinen Bruder.

blocks.content: Comparative: adjective + -er. Superlative: am … -sten or der/die/das … -ste. Umlaut often appears on a/o/u in one-syllable adjectives.

groß → größer → am größten
gut → besser → am besten
viel → mehr → am meisten
Use superlative to express the highest degree. Predicate superlative uses am + -sten; attributive uses der/die/das + -ste.
Attributive adjectives (before a noun) take endings based on the preceding article. Strong declension: no article → more endings. Weak: after der/die/das → mostly -e/-en.
After ein-words (ein, kein, mein…) use mixed declension — the article shows gender/case, the adjective takes a simpler ending.
Plural adjectives after der/die: always -en in weak declension.
Use the four-question flowchart: (1) article present? (2) in default form? (3) singular? (4) does article show gender? — to pick the correct ending.

blocks.de: Mit unserem alten Auto fahren wir nach Wien.
blocks.note: unser- + dative ending on adjective and article
